claims.text: Optimized NiTi shape-memory alloys can exhibit a pronounced, tunable temperature-dependent plastic-deformation response.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can produce this tunable response by engineering the martensitic transformation.
NiTi is initially austenitic at higher temperatures.
The initially austenitic NiTi can transform to martensite upon cooling.
Tailored heating and cooling cycles can adjust the martensitic-transformation temperature and kinetics.
Controlled strain rates can adjust the martensitic-transformation temperature and kinetics.
The reversible phase change is activated over a temperature regime spanning below and above the transformation temperature.
The relevant microstructural mediator is a reversible switch between austenite and martensite.
Temperature changes trigger a reversible phase transformation in NiTi.
The phase transformation modifies dislocation mobility.
The phase transformation modifies the active deformation mechanisms.
Martensite provides enhanced plasticity because of its lower symmetry and increased number of available slip systems.
The austenite phase is stiffer than the martensite phase.
Ductility increases in the temperature regime where the martensitic transformation is active relative to single-phase regimes.
Yield strength changes in the temperature regime where the martensitic transformation is active relative to single-phase regimes.
Conventional metals and high-entropy alloys lacking a robust reversible transformation generally have less tunable plastic deformation.
Conventional metals and high-entropy alloys lacking a robust reversible transformation generally exhibit more temperature-independent plastic deformation.
The tunable response requires compositions and processing conditions that reliably induce a reversible martensitic transformation.
Departures from suitable processing parameters or alloy purity may reduce the magnitude or reproducibility of the response.
